Shadowdreamer (Shadowdreamer, H83)

Region (English scoring-table region): Serpentspine.

In brief: Lead an exiled Black Orc warband and conquer the Serpentspine through prophecy, dreamfire, and underground raids, ultimately following a dreamfire crusade against the Dwarves.

Narrative: High | Mission-tree length: Long (48 direct missions) | Mission-tree update: Locally supports EU4 v1.37.5.0; the 2026 official dev diary directly introduces the new tree | Distinctiveness: Very high | Waiting: High (purges and colonization) | Early pressure: Medium-high | Expansion capacity: High

A Dream Born of Exile

In 1444, Shadowdreamer is a Black Orc tribe of the Old Dookan faith, led by Zog Shadowdreamer. Its historical rival is the Skewered Drake (H73), associated with Gor Vazumbrog (I14). The H83 historical script records Zog as ruler from 1442; the local narrative separately says that prophetic visions led to his expulsion from Gor Vazumbrog by the Skewered Drake and his departure with other believers to found a warband. The ruler-record date must not be treated as the date of exile or state formation. The Chinese source article attributes more distant background to an offline Wiki account: the original Gor Vazumbrog warband entered the Middle Serpentspine in 894, after which a group of heretics was driven east and became Shadowdreamer. That account is not present in the English Wiki page checked here and remains unverified in this English-source check. [Local historical script] [Local narrative text] [Wiki material; claim not corroborated by checked English page]

This is not an Orcish take on restoring lost Dwarven holds. Zog turns dreams and prophecy into a system of mobilization. The mission tree gradually gives the warband control of passes, holds, and followers, then transforms it—under the same H83 Tag—into a dream hegemon, potentially followed by a dreamfire-crusade government. The changes to tribe, ruler, religious mobilization, and national mechanics form one continuous campaign, not several unrelated countries before and after. [Local scripts]

How Dreamfire Drives War

“Dreamfire” measures the country's commitment to the Crusade of Dreams. The government mechanic generates Dreamfire through fighting Dwarves, destroying Dwarven holds, and purging Dwarven populations, then converts it into military power and faster looting. The mechanic therefore continually pushes the player toward specific enemies rather than leaving every direction of expansion open. Dream-forging, underground ambushes, and special troops further turn ore and narrow mountain passes into military resources. [Local scripts] [Local narrative text]

Early missions organize the warband around survival, the Drahmgrall, and successors; later missions require control of more distant mountains and holds. The local H83 narrative describes Zog's expulsion and the warband's journey toward Gor Ozumbrog. The Chinese source article cites Official Dev Diary 115 as presenting this exile, the crossing of the Serpentspine, and the “purge the Dwarves” religious-state route as the central design arc; that diary was not independently checked in this bounded local-Mod/Wiki review. Current local localization includes the casus belli text, purge-related mission and reform text, and Dreamfire references. These sources support the narrative direction; this check does not independently establish every current mechanic or value. [Local scripts] [Local narrative text] [Chinese source article's attribution; not independently verified]

It is easy to misread this campaign as “get Dreamfire and keep pushing.” In practice, the early migration and securing of a base, the mid-game task of keeping the warband combat-ready, and the late-game management of extensive underground territory are different burdens. Dreamfire rewards destruction and purging, but a rising resource balance does not solve administrative problems; the player still has to wait for population changes, colonization, and control of holds. Expect a long campaign if you want to experience Zog's and his successors' story, not a brief Orcish raid. [Local scripts] [Community views]

The dream route also carries a particular narrative irony: exiles were first cast out over faith, then founded a state that denies another sapient people even the right to survive. Their early experience can explain the origins of their hostility toward Gor Vazumbrog and the Dwarves, but it does not excuse the later institutionalized purges. The checked English Wiki page is only a short country entry and does not substantiate the broader origin account; the assessment of genocidal policy here comes from current local missions, reforms, and localization, not from that Wiki page. [Wiki material] [Local scripts]

Two 2026 player posts find the opening Dreamfire mechanic and underground objectives distinctive, but both criticize the long late-game waits for purging and colonization. They are not guarantees about a current save. Players who dislike waiting for province-population processing and prefer a brisk campaign may find this tree especially tiresome. [Community views]

This is also the key difference between Shadowdreamer and other Black Orc countries: it does not merely ask the player to seize more holds; it locks specific targets, population policy, and Dreamfire income together. As the missions progress, it becomes harder to treat the most consequential policy as ignorable background text. This gives the country a strong identity while binding its mechanics tightly to their consequences. [Local scripts] [Local narrative text]

The Value Judgment Cannot Be Avoided

The darkness here does not come from the protagonists being Orcs, the game's classification of them as “monsters,” or their waging war. The missions and mechanics explicitly designate Dwarves—a people with full societies and personhood—as targets for purging, turn population disappearance into a source of national resources, and provide a casus belli aimed at “eliminating the Dwarves.” This is institutionalized denial of personhood and a systematic genocidal direction, and must be assessed by the same standard applied to every other sapient people. [Local scripts] [Local narrative text]

The v2.1 personality coordinates are Expansionism 94/100 | Autocracy 91/100 | Magic ↔ Artifice 93/100 (100 = Magic, 0 = Artifice; theme intensity 89/100) | Pluralism 5/100.

The v2.1 value score is Evil (4/100), with a trajectory of radicalization. Phase scores: Exiled Warband (Neutral, 35/100) → Dreamfire Crusade (Evil, 4/100). Current mechanics turn the purging of Dwarven populations and destruction of holds into Dreamfire income, while the casus belli and reform text openly advocate eliminating Dwarves. The score concerns institutionalized genocide, not Orcish identity or ordinary warfare. Phase scores: Exiled Warband (Neutral, 35/100) → Dreamfire Crusade (Evil, 4/100). The phase scores distinguish state formation from the crusade: early exile and survival do not mean that genocidal policy has already been fully carried out. But the later core route is explicit enough that “revenge” or “religious faith” cannot diminish its severity. Recommended for players seeking dark fantasy, Dreamfire as a resource, and high-intensity mountain conquest; players unwilling to engage with an ethnic-purge-centered loop or long waits for purging and colonization should avoid it. [Local scripts] [Community views]

The Wiki main page contains only an infobox; see the evidence page for source boundaries concerning people, mechanics, and value judgments.

National Ideas (Reference Appendix)

The following reproduces the current local national-idea text and script effects. Traditions apply when the set is adopted; the seven ideas unlock in sequence as the idea group is invested in; the ambition applies after all seven ideas are unlocked. Only national ideas themselves are listed; racial, government, and mission rewards are not folded into their values. A newly formed set of ideas does not automatically stack with the old set. Idea descriptions may recount history or describe future aspirations; they do not automatically mean that the described events have already occurred by 1444.

Shadowdreamer (H83) — Shadowdreamer Ideas

Tradition: Shadowdreamer Traditions

Effect: Movement speed: +15%; Land morale: +10%.

Idea 1: Kabir Drahm

When Zog Shadowdreamer was exiled and driven out of Gor Vazumbrog by the Skewered Drake it was for his heretic vision: In a strange prophetic dream he saw the world from the eyes of Dookan himself. Banished for heresy, he left with other believers in his Dream, the Great Dream, or Kabir Drahm in Orcish. It now serves as the unifying cause for Zog's warband as they find their way to the place revealed to him in the dream: The abandoned hold of Gor Ozumbrog.

Effect: Tolerance of the True Faith: +2.

Idea 2: Cavern Colonisation Command

With our Dream leading us ever closer to Gor Ozumbrog, we need to prepare the surrounding caves and caverns for our new country. To that end we will need to settle every nook and cranny, every last spot up to the hold of our desire.

Effect: Settler growth: +2000%.

Idea 3: Shadow Soldiers

The Sagah, the Shadow Soldiers of Shadowdreamer are a fearsome unit. Clad in black fabric with the symbol of the Dream, a closed eye behind a clenched fist on their back, they hide in the dark caverns. There they wait so that they can surprise their enemy suddenly without warning. With the Sagah supporting us, the shadows are no longer merely hiding places. Instead, the shadows can be turned into potential traps waiting eagerly to be sprung.

Effect: Infantry combat ability: +10%.

Idea 4: The Drahmgrall

The Drahmgrall are the Dream-Speakers of Shadowdreamer. These leading shamans are those that receive the visions coaxed forth by sleep that the orcs of Shadowdreamer depend on for spiritual guidance. They traverse the dreamscape where they see through Dookan's eyes and witness strange and otherworldly vistas: Frozen forests beneath rivers of molten rock, swords shattering on dangling cave moss, inexplicable lights dancing deep within the dark.

Effect: Missionary strength: +2%.

Idea 5: A Devoted People

Only through their faith in the Dream could the warband stay together during the exile from Gor Vazumbrog, animated by the purpose laid out for them in Dookan's Dream. This purpose urges them ever forward towards fulfilling the Dream, labouring towards the goal that not even the Drahmgrall can fathom for now. Still, their devotion keeps them going, united by faith.

Effect: Devotion: +1; Legitimacy: +1; Republican tradition: +0.3; Horde unity: +1.

Idea 6: Order of the Farun Chashm

The Order of the Farun Chashm are reclusive shamans and sages living as hermits on the borders of Shadowdreamer who meditate on matters of state and innovation. This order of recluses see themselves as the opposite face of the Kabir Drahm from the Drahmgrall, calling themselves the "Forgotten Eye" Rumours spread that the strictness of their adherence to the Dream is a matter of debate. In exchange for being left mostly to their own machinations, they offer their services to the government as occasional advisors by bringing in new ideas from beyond the country. Their less zealous demeanour also makes them more agreeable merchants and diplomats, where they can gather foreign knowledge and bring it back to their home.

Effect: Idea cost: -5%; Global institution spread: +10%.

Idea 7: Delving the Shadows

Before Shadowdreamer there was the Segbandal, an alliance of five dwarven holds. There, the dwarves had to share among themselves, exchanging goods and manpower. We have no need for that, we can use everything we produce ourselves. In the name of Dookan we claim these riches for ourselves, and only ourselves now. We will usurp the dwarven machinery's original purpose and bend them to our will. Mines, farmsteads, quarries, workshops, they will all serve Dookan.

Effect: Goods produced modifier: +10%.

Ambition: Shadowdreamer Ambition

Effect: Religious strength modifier: +10%.
